statement: For $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ put $Bf(z) = \pi^{-n/4}\int e^{-(z\cdot z + x\cdot x)/2 + \sqrt{2}\, z\cdot x} f(x)\,dx$ for $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$. Then $B$ is a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) from the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ onto the [Bargmann-Fock space](c:bargmann-fock-space) $\mathcal{F}_n$ of [entire functions](c:entire-function) $F$ with $\pi^{-n}\int |F|^2 e^{-|z|^2}\,dV < \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The domain is the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with Lebesgue measure, for an integer $n \ge 1$.
The target $\mathcal{F}_n$ is the [Bargmann-Fock space](c:bargmann-fock-space) of entire functions on $\mathbb{C}^n$ with finite Gaussian norm.

conclusion: The map $B$ is a linear bijection from $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ onto $\mathcal{F}_n$ with $\|Bf\| = \|f\|$.

proofs.name: Hermite basis to monomial basis
proofs.slogan: Send the Hermite basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to the monomial basis of the Fock space.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in multi-index notation $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^n$ with Hermite functions $h_\alpha$ and monomials $e_\alpha(z) = z^\alpha/\sqrt{\alpha!}$. Convergence of the kernel series is checked in $L^2$ for each fixed $z$.

roles.why: The Hermite functions form an orthonormal basis of the domain, so $B$ is fixed by its values on them.
The monomials form an orthonormal basis of the target, which makes $B$ onto.

steps.slogan: Expand the Gaussian kernel of $B$ in Hermite functions.
steps.detail: The generating function $\sum_k H_k(t)s^k/k! = e^{2ts - s^2}$ of the [Hermite polynomials](c:hermite-polynomial) gives $A(z,x) = \sum_\alpha e_\alpha(z)\, h_\alpha(x)$ for the kernel $A$ of $B$. For fixed $z$ the series converges in $L^2(dx)$, since $\sum_\alpha |z^\alpha|^2/\alpha! = e^{|z|^2}$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Compute $Bf$ as a power series with the Hermite coefficients of $f$.
steps.detail: The $h_\alpha$ are real and orthonormal, so $\int A(z,x)\,h_\beta(x)\,dx = e_\beta(z)$ and $Bf(z) = \sum_\alpha \langle f, h_\alpha\rangle e_\alpha(z)$. The coefficients are bounded by $\|f\|$, so Cauchy-Schwarz gives convergence for every $z$, and $Bf$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function).

steps.slogan: Show that the monomials $e_\alpha$ are orthonormal in the Fock space.
steps.detail: In polar coordinates $z_j = r_je^{i\theta_j}$ the angular integrals vanish for $\alpha \ne \beta$. For $\alpha = \beta$ the radial integral $\int_0^\infty r^{2k}e^{-r^2}\,2r\,dr = k!$ in each variable gives norm $1$ for the [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) $\pi^{-n}e^{-|z|^2}dV$.

steps.slogan: Show that every function of the Fock space is a series of monomials.
steps.detail: An entire $F$ has a Taylor series $\sum c_\alpha z^\alpha$ that converges uniformly on polydiscs. Orthogonality on polydiscs and $R \to \infty$ give $\|F\|^2 = \sum |c_\alpha|^2\alpha!$, so $F = \sum \langle F, e_\alpha\rangle e_\alpha$ in $\mathcal{F}_n$.

steps.slogan: Match the two orthonormal bases to see that $B$ is unitary.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $Bh_\alpha = e_\alpha$. The $h_\alpha$ are an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (completeness of Hermite functions), and the $e_\alpha$ are one of $\mathcal{F}_n$ by steps 3 and 4. A linear map that sends one orthonormal basis onto another is a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator).

concepts.c:unitary-operator: The theorem asserts unitarity, which the basis matching proves.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Both sides are Hilbert spaces with orthonormal bases to compare.
concepts.c:bargmann-fock-space: The target space, whose monomials form the matching basis.
concepts.c:entire-function: Elements of the Fock space are entire, so Taylor series apply.
concepts.c:hermite-polynomial: Their generating function expands the kernel into Hermite functions.
concepts.c:gaussian-measure: The Fock norm integrates against the Gaussian weight, which makes monomials orthonormal.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: Mapping one orthonormal basis onto another gives a unitary map.

source.note: Bargmann's Hermite-function proof (Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 14, 1961), as presented in Folland, Harmonic Analysis in Phase Space, chapter 1. Completeness of the Hermite functions is quoted.

statement: Let $(M,g)$ be a simply connected [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n$ whose [holonomy group](c:holonomy-group) $H$ acts irreducibly on the tangent space and which is not locally [symmetric](c:symmetric-space). Then $H$ is $SO(n)$, $U(n/2)$, $SU(n/2)$, $Sp(n/4)Sp(1)$, $Sp(n/4)$, $G_2$ (with $n = 7$) or $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ (with $n = 8$).

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is simply connected and carries a positive definite [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) metric $g$.
The holonomy representation of $H$ on $T_pM$ is [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation).
The manifold $M$ is not locally [symmetric](c:symmetric-space).

conclusion: The holonomy group $H$ is one of the seven groups of the list.

proofs.name: Transitivity on the sphere
proofs.slogan: A non-symmetric irreducible holonomy group acts transitively on the unit sphere, and the groups that do so form the list.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; Simons' transitivity theorem and the two algebraic exclusions rest on the cited work. Irreducibility rules out Riemannian products, and the dimension is $n \ge 2$.

roles.why: Simple connection makes $H$ connected, and curvature spans its Lie algebra.
Irreducibility is the hypothesis of Simons' theorem and of the sphere classification.
Non-symmetry rules out the non-transitive case, where $M$ would be symmetric.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a connected subgroup of $SO(n)$ whose algebra is spanned by curvature.
steps.detail: Simple connection makes the [holonomy group](c:holonomy-group) $H \subseteq SO(n)$ connected. By the Ambrose-Singer theorem its [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) is spanned by the curvature operators $R(X,Y)$ at $p$, and by the Bianchi identity the curvature lies in the space of curvature tensors with values in this algebra.

steps.slogan: Show that a non-transitive irreducible holonomy group forces a locally symmetric space.
steps.detail: Simons' transitivity theorem says that if $H$ acts irreducibly but not transitively on the unit sphere of $T_pM$, then $M$ is locally [symmetric](c:symmetric-space). Olmos proves it through the normal holonomy of orbits. Since $M$ is not symmetric, $H$ acts transitively on $S^{n-1}$.

steps.slogan: List the connected compact groups that act transitively on a sphere.
steps.detail: Montgomery and Samelson, and Borel, classified the connected compact [Lie groups](c:lie-group) acting transitively and effectively on spheres: $SO(n)$, $U(m)$, $SU(m)$, $Sp(m)$, $Sp(m)U(1)$, $Sp(m)Sp(1)$, $G_2$, $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(9)$. By step 2, $H$ is one of them.

steps.slogan: Remove the two groups that do not occur for non-symmetric metrics.
steps.detail: Berger's algebraic analysis of curvature tensors excludes $Sp(m)U(1)$. By Alekseevskii and Brown-Gray, holonomy $\mathrm{Spin}(9)$ forces a locally symmetric Cayley plane, which $M$ is not.

steps.slogan: Collect the surviving groups with their dimensions into the stated list.
steps.detail: What remains is $SO(n)$, $U(m)$ and $SU(m)$ with $n = 2m$, $Sp(m)Sp(1)$ and $Sp(m)$ with $n = 4m$, $G_2$ with $n = 7$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ with $n = 8$. This is the list of the theorem.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The theorem concerns the holonomy of a Riemannian metric.
concepts.c:holonomy-group: The group whose possible values the theorem lists.
concepts.c:symmetric-space: Non-symmetry is what forces transitivity on the sphere.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducible action on the tangent space is required by Simons' theorem.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The curvature spans the holonomy algebra, which fixes the group.
concepts.c:lie-group: The classification of transitive sphere actions is a theorem on compact Lie groups.

source.ref: C. Olmos, A geometric proof of the Berger Holonomy Theorem, Annals of Mathematics 161 (2005), 579-588
source.note: The steps follow Berger (Bull. Soc. Math. France 83, 1955) and Simons (Ann. of Math. 76, 1962); Olmos gives the geometric proof of the transitivity step.

statement: Candidate A gets $p$ votes and candidate B gets $q$ votes with $0 \le q < p$. If all $\binom{p+q}{p}$ orderings of the votes are equally likely, the probability that A is strictly ahead after every vote is $\frac{p-q}{p+q}$. Here $\binom{p+q}{p}$ is a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient).

hypotheses.text: Candidate A gets $p$ votes, candidate B gets $q$ votes, and $0 \le q < p$.
Every ordering of the $p+q$ votes is equally likely.

conclusion: The probability that A stays strictly ahead throughout the count is $(p-q)/(p+q)$.

proofs.name: Reflection of paths
proofs.slogan: Count the orderings in which A is not always ahead by reflecting the part of the path before its first tie.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $q = 0$, where the only ordering has A ahead throughout. An ordering is a path with step $+1$ for a vote for A and $-1$ for a vote for B.

roles.why: The inequality $p > q$ makes every path that starts with $-1$ end above $0$, so it touches $0$.
Equal likelihood turns the probability into a ratio of numbers of orderings.

steps.slogan: Count all orderings as paths with $p$ up-steps and $q$ down-steps.
steps.detail: An ordering is a choice of the $p$ places of the votes for A among $p+q$ places, so there are $\binom{p+q}{p}$ of them. A is strictly ahead throughout exactly when the path stays above $0$ after every step.

steps.slogan: Count the bad orderings that begin with a vote for B.
steps.detail: Each such ordering is bad, since the first partial sum is $-1$. It is fixed by the $p$ places of the votes for A among the last $p+q-1$ places, so there are $\binom{p+q-1}{p}$ of them.

steps.slogan: Match the bad orderings that begin with A to those that begin with B.
steps.detail: A path that starts with $+1$ and touches $0$ has a first visit to $0$. Swap every step before that visit. This is a [bijection](c:bijection) onto the paths that start with $-1$: each such path ends at $p-q>0$, so it reaches $0$, and swapping again returns the original.

steps.slogan: Divide the number of good orderings by the number of all orderings.
steps.detail: The bad orderings number $2\binom{p+q-1}{p}$. Since $\binom{p+q-1}{p} = \frac{q}{p+q}\binom{p+q}{p}$, the good fraction is $1 - \frac{2q}{p+q} = \frac{p-q}{p+q}$, and equal likelihood makes this the probability.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The number of orderings and of bad orderings are binomial coefficients.
concepts.c:bijection: The reflection pairs two sets of paths, so they have the same size.

source.note: The reflection argument of D. Andre (1887), as in Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, volume 1, chapter III.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite connected [directed graph](c:directed-graph) with an edge, in which each vertex $v$ has in-degree and out-degree both equal to $\deg v$. For every vertex $w$, the number of [Eulerian circuits](c:eulerian-circuit), counted up to rotation, is $t_w(G)\prod_v(\deg v - 1)!$, where $t_w(G)$ counts the [arborescences](c:arborescence) of $G$ rooted at $w$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a finite connected [directed graph](c:directed-graph), with loops and multiple edges allowed, and it has an edge.
Every vertex has in-degree equal to out-degree.

conclusion: The number of Eulerian circuits is $t_w(G)\prod_v(\deg v - 1)!$ for every vertex $w$.

proofs.name: Last-exit bijection
proofs.slogan: Match Eulerian circuits with pairs of a rooted arborescence and exit orders at the vertices, then count the pairs.
proofs.scope: Circuits are counted up to rotation, so each has one rotation that starts with a fixed edge $e$ at the root $w$. Connectedness and one edge make every degree positive.

roles.why: Connectedness and an edge give every vertex positive degree and let the walk reach every vertex.
Equal in- and out-degrees force the walk to stop only at the root.

steps.slogan: Fix a root $w$ and an edge $e$ that leaves $w$.
steps.detail: Each [Eulerian circuit](c:eulerian-circuit) uses $e$ exactly once, so it has exactly one rotation that starts with $e$. Hence the number of circuits equals the number of Eulerian circuits that start with $e$.

steps.slogan: Record the exit order at each vertex and the last exit edges.
steps.detail: For a circuit that starts with $e$, list the out-edges of each $v$ in the order of use, giving an order $\sigma_v$ with $e$ first at $w$. For $v \ne w$ let $T(v)$ be the last edge of $\sigma_v$. The time of the last exit grows along $T$ and the circuit ends at $w$, so $T$ is an [arborescence](c:arborescence) rooted at $w$.

steps.slogan: Walk along given exit orders and show that the walk stops only at $w$.
steps.detail: Given $T$ and orders $\sigma_v$ with $e$ first at $w$ and $T(v)$ last at $v \ne w$, start at $w$ with $e$ and leave each vertex by its next unused edge. A vertex $v \ne w$ is entered at most $\deg v$ times and left one time fewer, so an unused out-edge remains and the walk cannot stop there.

steps.slogan: Show that the walk uses every edge, by following the last-exit edges.
steps.detail: The walk stops at $w$ after all $\deg w$ out-edges, so it entered $w$ $\deg w$ times and used every in-edge of $w$. Suppose some edge is unused. Then some $v \ne w$ has an unused out-edge, so $T(v)$ is unused, and its head has an unused in-edge and so an unused out-edge. Following $T$ ends at an unused in-edge of $w$, which is a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Count the pairs to get the product formula.
steps.detail: The two constructions are inverse [bijections](c:bijection) between circuits that start with $e$ and pairs of an arborescence $T$ with orders $\sigma_v$. There are $t_w(G)$ choices of $T$, $(\deg w - 1)!$ orders at $w$ after $e$, and $(\deg v - 1)!$ orders at each $v \ne w$ with $T(v)$ last. The product is $t_w(G)\prod_v(\deg v - 1)!$.

concepts.c:directed-graph: The graph is directed, so exits and entries at a vertex are distinct.
concepts.c:eulerian-circuit: The objects counted: closed walks that use every edge once.
concepts.c:arborescence: The last exit edges form an arborescence rooted at the start vertex.
concepts.c:bijection: Circuits and pairs correspond one to one, so their numbers agree.

source.note: The proof of van Aardenne-Ehrenfest and de Bruijn (1951) with Smith and Tutte, as in Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, volume 2, section 5.6.

statement: Let $\gamma$ be a [holomorphic matrix function](c:holomorphic-matrix-function) with values in $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ on an annulus $r < |z| < R$ with $r < 1 < R$. Then $\gamma = \gamma_-\,\lambda\,\gamma_+$, where $\gamma_+$ is holomorphic and invertible on $|z| < R$, $\gamma_-$ is holomorphic and invertible on $|z| > r$ including $\infty$, and $\lambda = \mathrm{diag}(z^{k_1},\dots,z^{k_n})$ with integers $k_i$ unique up to order.

hypotheses.text: The map $\gamma$ is a [holomorphic matrix function](c:holomorphic-matrix-function) on the annulus $r < |z| < R$ with values in $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$.

conclusion: The loop $\gamma$ factors as $\gamma_-\lambda\gamma_+$ with the stated factors, and the integers $k_i$ are unique up to order.

proofs.name: Clutching and Grothendieck splitting
proofs.slogan: Glue a bundle on the Riemann sphere from the loop, split it into line bundles, and compare the trivializations on the two discs.
proofs.scope: An outline: the splitting theorem of Grothendieck for bundles on the sphere is the cited ingredient, and it covers every $n \ge 1$. For $n = 1$ the integer $k$ is the winding number of $\gamma$ on the unit circle, and $\gamma$ is an element of the analytic [loop group](c:loop-group).

roles.why: The holomorphic loop is the transition function that defines a holomorphic bundle on the sphere.

steps.slogan: Glue two trivial bundles over the two discs of the sphere by $\gamma$.
steps.detail: Cover the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere) by $U_+ = \{|z| < R\}$ and $U_- = \{|z| > r\} \cup \{\infty\}$. Glue $U_+ \times \mathbb{C}^n$ and $U_- \times \mathbb{C}^n$ over the annulus by $s_- = \gamma s_+$. This defines a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) $E_\gamma$ of rank $n$.

steps.slogan: Split the bundle into line bundles by Grothendieck's theorem.
steps.detail: Grothendieck's theorem says that every holomorphic vector bundle on the Riemann sphere is isomorphic to a sum $\mathcal{O}(k_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \mathcal{O}(k_n)$ of line bundles. So $E_\gamma \cong \bigoplus \mathcal{O}(k_i)$ for some integers $k_i$.

steps.slogan: Write the isomorphism in trivializations over the two discs.
steps.detail: Each $\mathcal{O}(k)$ has holomorphic trivializations over $U_+$ and $U_-$ with transition function $z^k$. In them the isomorphism becomes invertible holomorphic matrices $g_+$ on $U_+$ and $h_-$ on $U_-$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two descriptions over the annulus to get the factorization.
steps.detail: Over the annulus the isomorphism respects the gluing, so $h_-\gamma = \lambda g_+$ with $\lambda = \mathrm{diag}(z^{k_i})$. Put $\gamma_- = h_-^{-1}$ and $\gamma_+ = g_+$ to get $\gamma = \gamma_-\lambda\gamma_+$.

steps.slogan: Read the integers $k_i$ from the splitting type to show they are unique.
steps.detail: Any factorization of $\gamma$ gives an isomorphism of $E_\gamma$ with $\bigoplus \mathcal{O}(k_i)$ by the reverse of steps 3 and 4. The multiset $\{k_i\}$ is an invariant of the bundle, for example through the dimensions of the spaces of sections of $E_\gamma \otimes \mathcal{O}(m)$. So the $k_i$ agree up to order.

concepts.c:holomorphic-matrix-function: The loop $\gamma$ is the data that is factored.
concepts.c:loop-group: The loop $\gamma$ is an element of the loop group $LGL_n(\mathbb{C})$.
concepts.c:riemann-sphere: The two discs of the sphere carry the two trivial bundles.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The glued object whose splitting type gives the diagonal factor.

source.ref: A. Grothendieck, Sur la classification des fibres holomorphes sur la sphere de Riemann, American Journal of Mathematics 79 (1957), 121-138
source.note: G. D. Birkhoff (Math. Ann. 74, 1913) proved the factorization directly; Pressley and Segal, Loop Groups (1986), treat smooth loops. The steps follow the bundle route.

statement: If $G$ is a finite group of order $p^aq^b$ with $p$ and $q$ prime and $a, b \ge 0$, then $G$ is [solvable](c:solvable-group).

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite.
The order of $G$ is $p^aq^b$ with $p$ and $q$ prime and $a, b \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Characters and a class of prime-power size
proofs.slogan: A minimal counterexample is simple, and a character argument on a class of prime-power size gives it a nontrivial center.
proofs.scope: Induction on $|G|$ for a non-solvable group of least order. A group with $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, or with $p = q$, is a $p$-group and solvable.

roles.why: Finiteness gives complex characters, their orthogonality relations and Sylow subgroups.
The order makes a Sylow $q$-subgroup of index $p^a$, so a central element of it has a class of $p$-power size.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a simple non-abelian group of order $p^aq^b$ with $a, b \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Take a non-solvable group of this form with least order. A proper normal subgroup $N$ and the quotient $G/N$ have smaller orders of the same form, so they are solvable, and then so is $G$. Hence $G$ is [simple](c:simple-group) and non-abelian. A $p$-group is solvable, so $a, b \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Choose an element whose conjugacy class has prime-power size above one.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $q$-subgroup and take $1 \ne g \in Z(Q)$, which exists by the class equation. Then $Q \le C_G(g)$, so the class of $g$ has size $|G : C_G(g)|$ dividing $p^a$. The size is above $1$ because $Z(G) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Find a nontrivial character of degree prime to $p$ that does not vanish at $g$.
steps.detail:
Column orthogonality gives $0 = 1 + \sum_{\chi 
e 1}\chi(1)\chi(g)$ over the irreducible [characters](c:character-of-a-representation). If $\chi(g) = 0$ whenever $p 
mid \chi(1)$, then $-1/p = \sum  rac{\chi(1)}{p}\chi(g)$ would be an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer), which is false. So some $\chi 
e 1$ has $p 
mid \chi(1)$ and $\chi(g) 
e 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the representation of $\chi$ sends $g$ to a scalar matrix.
steps.detail: The class size is a power of $p$ and $p \nmid \chi(1)$, so Bezout shows that $\alpha = \chi(g)/\chi(1)$ is an algebraic integer. As an average of roots of unity, $\alpha$ and its conjugates have modulus at most $1$, and its norm is a nonzero integer, so $|\alpha| = 1$. Hence all eigenvalues of $\rho(g)$ are equal and $\rho(g)$ is scalar.

steps.slogan: Derive a nontrivial center to contradict simplicity.
steps.detail: The kernel of $\rho$ is a normal subgroup, proper because $\chi \ne 1$, so $\rho$ is faithful. The scalar $\rho(g)$ commutes with $\rho(G)$, so $1 \ne g \in Z(G)$. This contradicts $Z(G) = 1$, so every group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable.

concepts.c:solvable-group: The property to prove, reached by showing that no minimal counterexample exists.
concepts.c:simple-group: A minimal counterexample has no proper normal subgroup, so it is simple.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: A Sylow $q$-subgroup has a central element with a class of $p$-power size.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: Character values and their orthogonality detect the central element.
concepts.c:algebraic-integer: Character values are algebraic integers, which rules out $1/p$ and bounds moduli.

source.note: Burnside's 1904 character-theoretic argument, as in Isaacs, Character Theory of Finite Groups (1976), chapter 3.

statement: Any two nonempty [countable](c:countable-set) [dense linear orders without endpoints](c:dlo) are order-isomorphic.

hypotheses.text: Both orders $A$ and $B$ are [countable](c:countable-set).
Both orders are [dense linear orders](c:dense-linear-order): between any two elements there is a third.
Both orders are nonempty and have no least element and no greatest element.

conclusion: There is an order-preserving bijection from $A$ onto $B$.

proofs.name: Back and forth
proofs.slogan: Extend finite partial isomorphisms one point at a time, alternating between the two orders, and take the union.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Nonemptiness lets the extension step start from the empty partial isomorphism.

roles.why: Countability lists all points of both orders in one sequence, so each point is handled once.
Density gives a point strictly between two images.
Having no endpoints, and being nonempty, gives a point above, below or beside any finite set of images.

steps.slogan: Define partial isomorphisms as finite order-preserving matchings.
steps.detail: A partial isomorphism is a finite set $f$ of pairs $(a, b)$ with $a < a'$ if and only if $b < b'$ for any two pairs. Order them by inclusion. The empty set is one.

steps.slogan: Extend any partial isomorphism to include a given point of $A$.
steps.detail: Let $a \in A$ be outside the domain of $f$. The images of the pairs below $a$ lie below the images of the pairs above $a$. Density, no endpoints and nonemptiness of $B$ give $b \in B$ strictly between them, and $f \cup \{(a, b)\}$ is a partial isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Extend any partial isomorphism to include a given point of $B$.
steps.detail: The inverse relation of $f$ is a partial isomorphism from $B$ to $A$. Apply the previous step with the roles of the two orders exchanged, which is allowed because $A$ is also dense, nonempty and without endpoints.

steps.slogan: Enumerate both orders and build an increasing chain of partial isomorphisms.
steps.detail: List $A \sqcup B$ as $c_0, c_1, \dots$, which is possible by countability. Let $f_0 = \emptyset$ and choose $f_{k+1} \supseteq f_k$ with $c_k$ in its domain or range, by the two extension steps. This is the [back-and-forth method](c:back-and-forth).

steps.slogan: Show that the union of the chain is an order isomorphism.
steps.detail: Let $F = \bigcup_k f_k$. Two pairs of $F$ lie in a common $f_k$, so $F$ preserves and reflects order, hence is an injective function. Every $a \in A$ lies in a domain and every $b \in B$ in a range, so $F$ is total and onto.

concepts.c:countable-set: A list of all points makes the construction reach each point.
concepts.c:dlo: The theorem concerns dense linear orders without endpoints.
concepts.c:dense-linear-order: Density supplies the new image point between two old ones.
concepts.c:back-and-forth: The construction alternates between extending the domain and the range.

source.note: mathlib uses finite partial isomorphisms (PartialIso), the extension lemma exists_across, the cofinal sets definedAtLeft and definedAtRight, and an ideal that meets all of them (idealOfCofinals).

statement: Over a fixed relational schema and finite instances, a query is expressible in [relational algebra](c:relational-algebra) if and only if a domain-independent [relational calculus](c:relational-calculus) formula expresses it.

hypotheses.text: Queries are over a fixed schema with finite instances, and the algebra has selection, projection, product, union, difference, renaming and constants.
The calculus formula is domain independent: its answer on an instance does not change when the domain grows beyond the active domain and its constants.

conclusion: The algebra and the domain-independent calculus define the same queries.

proofs.name: Translation in both directions
proofs.slogan: Translate algebra into calculus by induction on expressions, and domain-independent calculus into algebra over the active domain.
proofs.scope: Queries map finite instances to finite relations. The calculus is first-order logic with equality and constants.

roles.why: The operators of the algebra are exactly those that the formula translation uses.
Domain independence lets all quantifiers range over the finite active domain.

steps.slogan: Translate each algebra operator into a calculus formula by induction.
steps.detail: A relation name gives an atom, selection adds a condition by $\wedge$, projection adds $\exists$, product and join give $\wedge$, union gives $\vee$, and difference gives $\varphi \wedge \neg\psi$. Each free variable occurs in a positive atom or constant, so the formula is domain independent and computes the expression.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the domain-independent formula over the active domain.
steps.detail: Let $D$ be the active domain of the instance with the constants of $\varphi$. By domain independence, the answer over $D$ equals the answer over any larger domain. So the answer is that of $\varphi$ with every quantifier ranging over $D$.

steps.slogan: Express the active domain as an algebra expression.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{Adom}$ be the union of the projections of every column of every relation and of the constant singletons of $\varphi$. Its value is $D$, and $\mathrm{Adom}^k$ is a product of $k$ copies.

steps.slogan: Translate the formula into algebra by induction on its structure.
steps.detail: For a formula with $k$ free variables, build an expression with values in $D^k$. Atoms and equalities give relations with selections, $\wedge$ gives a join, and $\vee$ pads both sides with $\mathrm{Adom}$ and takes the union. Negation gives $\mathrm{Adom}^k$ minus the value, and $\exists x$ gives a projection.

steps.slogan: Combine the two translations into the equivalence of the languages.
steps.detail: Step 1 puts every algebra query into the calculus. Steps 2 to 4 give an algebra expression with the same answer as each domain-independent formula. So the two languages define the same queries.

concepts.c:relational-algebra: One side of the equivalence, built from a few operators.
concepts.c:relational-calculus: The other side of the equivalence, written as first-order formulas.

source.note: Codd (1972), Relational completeness of data base sublanguages; the textbook proof in Abiteboul, Hull and Vianu, Foundations of Databases (1995), on the algebra and calculus.

statement: For every complex number $z$ the [power series](c:power-series) $\sum_{n \ge 0}(-1)^n z^{2n}/(2n)!$ converges, and its sum is $\cos z$.

hypotheses.text: The number $z$ is a complex number.

proofs.name: Mean of two exponential series
proofs.slogan: Write the cosine as the mean of two exponentials and add their power series.
proofs.scope: All complex $z$; the real case is the restriction to real $z$. The odd-degree terms cancel.

roles.why: The exponential series converges for every complex number, so $z$ needs no restriction.

steps.slogan: Write $\cos z$ as the mean of $e^{iz}$ and $e^{-iz}$.
steps.detail: By Euler's formula, $e^{\pm iz} = \cos z \pm i\sin z$, so $\cos z = (e^{iz} + e^{-iz})/2$. This holds for every complex $z$.

steps.slogan: Expand both exponentials in their power series.
steps.detail: The [exponential function](c:exponential-function) has the [power series](c:power-series) $e^w = \sum_{m \ge 0} w^m/m!$, which converges for every $w \in \mathbb{C}$. Apply it to $w = iz$ and to $w = -iz$.

steps.slogan: Add the two series term by term and halve.
steps.detail: Convergent series add termwise. The term of index $m$ is $((iz)^m + (-iz)^m)/(2\,m!)$, which is $0$ for odd $m$ and $(iz)^m/m!$ for even $m$.

steps.slogan: Replace $(iz)^{2n}$ by $(-1)^n z^{2n}$ in the even terms.
steps.detail: For $m = 2n$ we have $(iz)^{2n} = (i^2)^n z^{2n} = (-1)^n z^{2n}$. So the series has the term $(-1)^n z^{2n}/(2n)!$ at place $2n$ and $0$ at odd places.

steps.slogan: Drop the zero odd terms to get the series in $n$.
steps.detail: A convergent series whose odd-indexed terms are zero has the sum of its even-indexed terms. Hence $\sum_n (-1)^n z^{2n}/(2n)!$ converges, with sum $\cos z$.

concepts.c:power-series: The cosine series and the exponential series are both power series.
concepts.c:exponential-function: Its series, taken at $\pm iz$, produces the cosine series.

source.note: mathlib adds the exponential series (expSeries_div_hasSum_exp) at $zi$ and $-zi$ in hasSum_cos', keeps the even places, and rewrites $(zi)^{2n}$ as $(-1)^n z^{2n}$.

statement: Let $L \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) with $d \in \{2, 3\}$, and let $R$ be a [rotation](c:rotation-matrix) of finite order $n$ with $R(L) = L$. Then $n \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $L$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of rank $d$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $d = 2$ or $d = 3$.
The map $R$ is a [rotation](c:rotation-matrix) of $\mathbb{R}^d$ of finite order $n$ with $R(L) = L$.

conclusion: The order $n$ of the rotation is $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$ or $6$.

proofs.name: Integer trace
proofs.slogan: In a lattice basis the rotation is an integer matrix, so its trace is an integer that restricts the angle.
proofs.scope: The rotation has angle $\theta$ about the origin ($d = 2$) or about an axis ($d = 3$), and the identity is included. The order of $R$ is the [order](c:order-of-an-element) of $\theta$ in $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.

roles.why: A basis of the lattice gives coordinates in which $R$ has integer entries.
The trace of a rotation depends only on its angle, and its order fixes the angle.

steps.slogan: Write $R$ as an integer matrix in a lattice basis.
steps.detail: Let $b_1, \dots, b_d$ be a basis of $L$. Since $R(L) = L$, each $Rb_j$ is an integer combination of the $b_i$. So the matrix $M$ of $R$ in this basis has integer entries.

steps.slogan: Compute the trace of $M$ from the rotation angle.
steps.detail: The [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) does not depend on the basis, so $\operatorname{tr} M = \operatorname{tr} R$. This is $2\cos\theta$ for $d = 2$ and $1 + 2\cos\theta$ for $d = 3$. In both cases $\operatorname{tr} M$ is an integer.

steps.slogan: Limit $2\cos\theta$ to the integers from $-2$ to $2$.
steps.detail: In both cases $2\cos\theta$ is an integer, because it is $\operatorname{tr} M$ or $\operatorname{tr} M - 1$. Also $|2\cos\theta| \le 2$. So $\cos\theta \in \{-1, -\tfrac12, 0, \tfrac12, 1\}$.

steps.slogan: List the angles with these cosines and read off their orders.
steps.detail: These cosines give $\theta \in \{0, \pi, \pm\pi/2, \pm\pi/3, \pm 2\pi/3\}$ modulo $2\pi$. Their orders in $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ are $1, 2, 4, 6, 3$. The order of $R$ equals the order of $\theta$, so $n \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\}$.

concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: A lattice basis turns the symmetry into an integer matrix.
concepts.c:rotation-matrix: The rotation has a trace that depends only on its angle.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The trace is basis independent, so it is an integer and also $2\cos\theta$ or $1 + 2\cos\theta$.
concepts.c:order-of-an-element: The order of the rotation is the order of its angle.

source.note: The classical trace argument of crystallography; see for example Senechal, Quasicrystals and Geometry (1995).

statement: For a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ and integers $p, q \ge 0$, the [Dolbeault cohomology](c:dolbeault-cohomology) group $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X)$ is isomorphic to the [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) group $H^q(X, \Omega^p)$ of the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold), Hausdorff and second countable.

proofs.name: Fine resolution
proofs.slogan: Resolve the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms by fine sheaves of smooth $(p, q)$-forms and read cohomology from the global sections.
proofs.scope: All $p, q \ge 0$. The local solution of the $\bar\partial$-equation is the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma; the rest is sheaf theory.

roles.why: Holomorphic charts give polydiscs for the local lemma, and paracompactness gives partitions of unity.

steps.slogan: Solve the $\bar\partial$-equation on a polydisc.
steps.detail: By the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma, on a polydisc every $\bar\partial$-closed $(p, q)$-form with $q \ge 1$ is $\bar\partial$-exact. The proof removes the variables $\bar z_j$ one at a time with the Cauchy transform in one variable.

steps.slogan: Show that the Dolbeault complex of sheaves resolves $\Omega^p$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{A}^{p,q}$ be the sheaf of smooth $(p, q)$-forms. The kernel of $\bar\partial$ on $\mathcal{A}^{p,0}$ is $\Omega^p$ by the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Exactness at $\mathcal{A}^{p,q}$ for $q \ge 1$ is step 1 on stalks, so $0 \to \Omega^p \to \mathcal{A}^{p,0} \to \mathcal{A}^{p,1} \to \cdots$ is exact.

steps.slogan: Show that each sheaf $\mathcal{A}^{p,q}$ is fine and has no higher cohomology.
steps.detail: The [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\mathcal{A}^{p,q}$ is a module over the sheaf of smooth functions, so smooth [partitions of unity](c:partition-of-unity) make it fine. A fine sheaf has $H^k(X, \mathcal{A}^{p,q}) = 0$ for $k \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Compute the cohomology of $\Omega^p$ from the global sections of the resolution.
steps.detail: A resolution by acyclic sheaves computes sheaf cohomology. By the long exact sequences of its short exact pieces, $H^q(X, \Omega^p)$ is the $q$-th cohomology of the complex $\Gamma(X, \mathcal{A}^{p,\bullet})$.

steps.slogan: Identify that complex of global sections with the Dolbeault complex.
steps.detail: The global sections $\Gamma(X, \mathcal{A}^{p,q})$ are the smooth $(p, q)$-forms on $X$, and the differential is $\bar\partial$. Its cohomology is $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X)$, so $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X) \cong H^q(X, \Omega^p)$.

concepts.c:complex-manifold: Local holomorphic charts and a global smooth structure are both needed.
concepts.c:dolbeault-cohomology: The cohomology of global smooth forms under $\bar\partial$, one side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The other side, computed through an acyclic resolution.
concepts.c:sheaf: The forms and the holomorphic forms are sheaves on $X$.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: It makes the sheaves of smooth forms fine, hence acyclic.

source.note: The standard proof as in Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry (1978), chapter 0, which cites the Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma.

statement: Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be an adapted integrable process on a [filtered probability space](c:filtered-probability-space). Then $X_n = M_n + A_n$ for a [martingale](c:martingale) $M$ and a [predictable process](c:predictable-process) $A$ with $A_0 = 0$, and this decomposition is unique almost surely.

hypotheses.text: Each $X_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable.
Each $X_n$ is integrable.

conclusion: There are a martingale $M$ and a predictable process $A$ with $A_0 = 0$ and $X = M + A$, unique up to null sets.

proofs.name: Sum of conditional increments
proofs.slogan: Add the conditional expected increments to build the predictable part, and prove uniqueness because a predictable martingale from zero is zero.
proofs.scope: Discrete time $n \ge 0$. Predictable means that $A_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable for $n \ge 1$, and equalities hold almost surely.

roles.why: Adaptedness makes $M_n = X_n - A_n$ adapted and each conditional increment $\mathcal{F}_{k-1}$-measurable.
Integrability makes the conditional expectations exist and keeps $A_n$ and $M_n$ integrable.

steps.slogan: Define the predictable part as the sum of conditional expected increments.
steps.detail: Put $A_0 = 0$ and $A_n = \sum_{k=1}^n E[X_k - X_{k-1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}]$. By integrability, each term is a [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) that is defined and integrable. Each term is $\mathcal{F}_{k-1}$-measurable, so $A_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable.

steps.slogan: Show that the difference $M_n = X_n - A_n$ is a martingale.
steps.detail: The process $M$ is adapted and integrable. Since $A_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, $E[M_n - M_{n-1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}] = E[X_n - X_{n-1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}] - (A_n - A_{n-1}) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Compare two decompositions through the difference of their martingale parts.
steps.detail: Let $X = M' + A'$ be another such decomposition. Then $D_n = M_n - M'_n = A'_n - A_n$ is a martingale with $D_0 = 0$, and it is predictable because $A_n$ and $A'_n$ are.

steps.slogan: Show that a predictable martingale that starts at zero is zero.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 1$, $D_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, so $D_n = E[D_n \mid \mathcal{F}_{n-1}] = D_{n-1}$ almost surely by the martingale property. Induction from $D_0 = 0$ gives $D_n = 0$ for all $n$, so $M = M'$ and $A = A'$ almost surely.

concepts.c:filtered-probability-space: The filtration $\mathcal{F}_n$ defines adaptedness and predictability.
concepts.c:martingale: The martingale part is the process minus its predictable drift.
concepts.c:predictable-process: The drift is known one step ahead, so it is predictable.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: The drift adds up the conditional expectations of the increments.

source.note: The standard proof, as in Williams, Probability with Martingales (1991), in the section on the Doob decomposition.

statement: Let $S$ be a right-continuous submartingale of class (D) on $[0, T]$ for a filtration with the usual conditions. Then $S = M + A$ with $M$ a uniformly integrable [martingale](c:martingale) and $A$ an increasing [predictable process](c:predictable-process) with $A_0 = 0$. The decomposition is unique up to indistinguishability.

hypotheses.text: The process $S$ is a right-continuous submartingale.
The process $S$ has class (D): the variables $S_\tau$ over stopping times $\tau \le T$ are [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability).
The [filtration](c:filtration) is right-continuous and complete.

conclusion: $S = M + A$ with $M$ a uniformly integrable martingale and $A$ increasing, predictable and integrable, unique up to indistinguishability.

proofs.name: Dyadic decompositions and Komlos limits
proofs.slogan: Take discrete Doob decompositions on dyadic times, keep their increasing parts compact in $L^1$ by class (D), and pass to a limit through convex combinations.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published short proof; the uniform integrability estimate, the Komlos limit and the predictability of the limit rest on the cited work. The horizon $T$ is finite.

roles.why: The submartingale property makes each discrete compensator increasing.
Class (D) makes the terminal values of the compensators uniformly integrable, so limits exist in $L^1$.
The usual conditions allow right-continuous modifications and the notion of predictability.

steps.slogan: Apply the discrete Doob decomposition on dyadic times.
steps.detail: For each $n$, sample $S$ at the times $jT2^{-n}$ and write $S = M^n + A^n$ there. The part $A^n$ is predictable in discrete time, and it is increasing because $S$ is a submartingale.

steps.slogan: Show that class (D) makes the values $A^n_T$ uniformly integrable.
steps.detail: The cited proof stops $A^n$ at the first time it exceeds a level $c$ and uses class (D) to bound $E[A^n_T;\, A^n_T > c]$ uniformly in $n$. So $(A^n_T)_n$ is bounded and [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability) in $L^1$.

steps.slogan: Pass to convex combinations that converge in $L^1$ by a Komlos-type lemma.
steps.detail: Uniform integrability and a Komlos-type lemma give convex combinations of the tails $(A^m_T)_{m \ge n}$ that converge in $L^1$ to some $A_T$. The same weights applied to $A^m_t$ at dyadic times give limits $A_t$.

steps.slogan: Define the limit process and the martingale part.
steps.detail: At dyadic times the limits $A_t$ are increasing in $t$, and a right-continuous modification is taken. Put $M = S - A$. The cited argument shows that $M$ is a uniformly integrable [martingale](c:martingale), since each $M^m$ is one and the limits are in $L^1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit process $A$ is predictable.
steps.detail: The cited proof shows that $A$ is predictable, as a limit of convex combinations of the predictable approximations $A^n$. Together with step 4 this gives the decomposition $S = M + A$.

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness: a predictable martingale of finite variation from zero is zero.
steps.detail: If $M + A = M' + A'$, then $M - M' = A' - A$ is a [predictable](c:predictable-process) martingale of finite variation that starts at $0$. Such a process vanishes, so the decomposition is unique up to indistinguishability.

concepts.c:martingale: The martingale part is the submartingale minus its increasing part.
concepts.c:predictable-process: The increasing part must be predictable for the decomposition to be unique.
concepts.c:uniform-integrability: It gives compactness of the compensators in $L^1$.
concepts.c:filtration: Right-continuity and completeness of the filtration support the limits and predictability.

source.ref: M. Beiglbock, W. Schachermayer and B. Veliyev, A short proof of the Doob-Meyer theorem, Stochastic Processes and their Applications 122 (2012), 1204-1209
source.note: The original is P.-A. Meyer, A decomposition theorem for supermartingales, Illinois J. Math. 6 (1962); this outline follows the short proof.

statement: Let $A$ be a subset of a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$. Then $A$ is [compact](c:compact-space) in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology) if and only if every sequence in $A$ has a subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $A$, if and only if every infinite subset of $A$ has a weak [limit point](c:limit-point) in $A$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), real or complex.
The set $A \subseteq X$ is an arbitrary subset.

conclusion: Weak compactness, weak sequential compactness and weak countable compactness of $A$ are equivalent.

proofs.name: Norming functionals (Whitley)
proofs.slogan: Prove the cycle of implications, using separable subspaces for one step and norming functionals for the hard step.
proofs.scope: Three implications close a cycle; the hard one is that countable compactness gives compactness. If $A$ is empty everything is trivial.

roles.why: Completeness gives the uniform boundedness principle, and the bidual with Banach-Alaoglu gives compactness.
The cycle proves compactness of $A$ itself, so $A$ needs no closedness assumption.

steps.slogan: Show that weak sequential compactness gives weak countable compactness.
steps.detail: Let $B \subseteq A$ be infinite and pick distinct $x_n \in B$. A subsequence converges weakly to some $x \in A$. Every weak neighborhood of $x$ then contains some $x_{n_j}$ different from $x$, so $x$ is a weak limit point of $B$.

steps.slogan: Show that weak compactness gives weak sequential compactness.
steps.detail: Let $(x_n)$ lie in a weakly compact $A$ and let $Y$ be the closed span of the $x_n$, which is separable. Hahn-Banach gives a countable norming set $\{\varphi_k\} \subseteq B_{X^*}$ for $Y$. The topology of pointwise convergence on $\{\varphi_k\}$ is metrizable on bounded sets, Hausdorff on $Y$ and weaker than the weak topology, so it agrees with it on the weak closure of $\{x_n\}$, a compact subset of $A$. A compact metrizable set is sequentially compact.

steps.slogan: Show that a weakly countably compact set is bounded in norm.
steps.detail: If $\varphi(A)$ were unbounded for some $\varphi \in X^*$, there would be distinct $x_n \in A$ with $|\varphi(x_n)| \to \infty$. Their set would have no weak limit point in $A$, since $\varphi$ is continuous. So every $\varphi(A)$ is bounded, and the uniform boundedness principle makes $A$ bounded.

steps.slogan: Build a sequence in $A$ close to a point of the weak-star closure.
steps.detail: Let $x^{**}$ be in the weak-star closure of $A$ in the [bidual](c:bidual). Choose $x_n \in A$ and finite sets $\Phi_1 \subseteq \Phi_2 \subseteq \cdots$ in $B_{X^*}$ such that $\Phi_n$ norms $E_n = \mathrm{span}\{x^{**} - x_1, \dots, x^{**} - x_n\}$ up to a factor $2$, and $|\varphi(x_{n+1}) - x^{**}(\varphi)| < 1/n$ for $\varphi \in \Phi_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that a weak cluster point of the sequence agrees with $x^{**}$ on the norming sets.
steps.detail: By countable compactness the sequence has a weak cluster point $x \in A$, or a value taken infinitely often. For $\varphi \in \Phi_p$ and all $n \ge p$ we have $|\varphi(x_{n+1}) - x^{**}(\varphi)| < 1/n$, so $\varphi(x) = x^{**}(\varphi)$.

steps.slogan: Use the norming sets to show that $x^{**}$ equals the point $x$ of $A$.
steps.detail: By Mazur's theorem $x$ is a norm limit of convex combinations of the $x_n$, so $x^{**} - x$ lies in the closure of $\bigcup E_n$. On that closure the union $\Phi$ of the $\Phi_n$ still norms up to $2$, and $x^{**} - x$ vanishes on $\Phi$. Hence $x^{**} = x \in A$.

steps.slogan: Close the cycle of implications with the Banach-Alaoglu theorem.
steps.detail: Step 6 shows that the weak-star closure of $A$ lies in $A$. By step 3 and Banach-Alaoglu this closure is [weak-star](c:weak-star-topology) compact, and the weak topology of $X$ is the restriction of the weak-star topology. So countable compactness gives compactness, and with steps 1 and 2 the three properties are equivalent.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness gives uniform boundedness and the bidual embedding.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness in the weak topology is one of the equivalent properties.
concepts.c:weak-topology: All three properties refer to the weak topology of $X$.
concepts.c:limit-point: Countable compactness asks for limit points of infinite subsets.
concepts.c:bidual: The weak-star closure of $A$ lives in the bidual.
concepts.c:weak-star-topology: Banach-Alaoglu gives compactness in the weak-star topology of the bidual.

source.note: After R. J. Whitley, An elementary proof of the Eberlein-Smulian theorem, Math. Ann. 172 (1967), 116-118, which uses norming sets of finitely many functionals.

statement: Let $M$ be a [module](c:module) over a commutative ring $R$. Then $M$ is [flat](c:flat-module) if and only if every relation $\sum_{i=1}^l f_i x_i = 0$ with $f_i \in R$ and $x_i \in M$ is trivial: there are $y_1, \dots, y_k \in M$ and $a_{ij} \in R$ with $x_i = \sum_j a_{ij} y_j$ for all $i$ and $\sum_i f_i a_{ij} = 0$ for all $j$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative and $M$ is an $R$-[module](c:module).

conclusion: The module $M$ is flat if and only if every relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial.

proofs.name: Ideals and relations
proofs.slogan: Test flatness on ideals, then turn a vanishing tensor into a trivial relation and back.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence for any commutative ring and any finite family $f_1, \dots, f_l$.

roles.why: Commutativity makes ideals $R$-modules and gives the isomorphism $R \otimes M \cong M$.

steps.slogan: Reduce flatness to injectivity of $I \otimes M \to M$ for all ideals.
steps.detail: The module $M$ is [flat](c:flat-module) if and only if $I \otimes_R M \to M$ is injective for every ideal $I$ of $R$. This ideal criterion is the first link of the mathlib proof, iff_rTensor_injective'.

steps.slogan: Present the ideal generated by $f_1, \dots, f_l$ by its relations.
steps.detail: Let $I = (f_1, \dots, f_l)$ and $K = \ker(R^l \to I,\ e_i \mapsto f_i)$. The sequence $K \to R^l \to I \to 0$ is [exact](c:exact-sequence), and the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) with $M$ is right exact, so $K \otimes M \to M^l \to I \otimes M \to 0$ is exact.

steps.slogan: Show that flatness makes every relation trivial.
steps.detail: A relation gives $x = (x_i) \in M^l$ with image $0$ in $M$ under $M^l \to I \otimes M \to M$. By injectivity, $x$ maps to $0$ in $I \otimes M$, so $x = \sum_j k_j \otimes y_j$ with $k_j = (a_{ij})_i \in K$. That is $x_i = \sum_j a_{ij}y_j$ and $\sum_i f_i a_{ij} = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that trivial relations give injectivity of $I \otimes M \to M$.
steps.detail: Let $t = \sum_i f_i \otimes x_i \in I \otimes M$ map to $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$. The relation is trivial, so $t = \sum_i f_i \otimes \sum_j a_{ij} y_j = \sum_j (\sum_i a_{ij} f_i) \otimes y_j = 0$ in $I \otimes M$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 3 shows that flat modules have only trivial relations. Steps 1 and 4 show that a module with only trivial relations is flat. So $M$ is flat if and only if every relation is trivial.

concepts.c:module: The statement concerns modules over a commutative ring.
concepts.c:flat-module: Flatness is the property that is tested on ideals and on relations.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The presentation of the ideal gives an exact sequence of modules.
concepts.c:tensor-product: Right exactness of the tensor product turns the presentation into a relation statement.

source.note: mathlib reads it off tfae_equational_criterion: flat, injectivity of I tensor M into M for all ideals (iff_rTensor_injective'), vanishing tensors vanish trivially, and trivial relations.
